questions.prompt: Put the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident response lifecycle, from Lesson 1, in their correct order.
questions.explain: NIST SP 800-61 draws these four phases as a cycle, not a line: Preparation happens before anything goes wrong, Detection & Analysis confirms and understands a real incident, Containment, Eradication & Recovery is the active response, and Post-Incident Activity is the lessons-learned review that feeds its findings back into Preparation, which is exactly what makes this a loop instead of a one-time checklist, as Lesson 1 explains.

questions.prompt: An incident starts and the team discovers nobody currently has the admin access needed to isolate the affected server, because whoever had that access left the company two months ago. Per Lesson 2, which NIST phase actually failed, and why isn't this a Detection & Analysis problem?
options: Preparation failed — ready tools and access are supposed to be provisioned, tested, and already known to work before any incident starts
Detection & Analysis failed — the team should have detected the access gap as part of confirming the incident
Containment, Eradication & Recovery failed — isolation is a containment action, so any isolation problem belongs to that phase
Post-Incident Activity failed — access reviews are something only a lessons-learned meeting is responsible for catching
questions.explain: Lesson 2 names this exact scenario as a Preparation failure: ready tools and access are one of Preparation's three required pieces, alongside a written plan and a trained team, and all three have to exist before the first alert fires, not be scrambled together during the incident.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines Containment, Eradication, and Recovery as the three distinct, sequential jobs Lesson 4 describes, rather than one action with three labels?
options: Containment limits an attacker's ability to do further damage right now; Eradication removes the actual cause so the problem can't simply resume; Recovery returns affected systems to verified-clean, normal operation
Containment removes the actual cause of the incident; Eradication limits further damage; Recovery documents what happened for the after-action report
Containment, Eradication, and Recovery are three names for the same action, performed once, with no required order between them
Containment restores systems to production; Eradication isolates the attacker; Recovery removes the root cause
Containment is the lessons-learned review; Eradication is the technical cleanup; Recovery is the executive notification
Containment and Eradication happen simultaneously, and Recovery can happen before either one finishes
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is explicit that these are three separate jobs done in sequence: Containment stops the bleeding, Eradication removes the actual cause, and Recovery returns systems to verified-clean normal operation — and the order matters because each phase depends on the one before it actually being finished.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps Containment's and Eradication's definitions backwards — it's Eradication that removes the actual cause, while Containment is the fast action that limits further damage. Lesson 4 warns specifically against attempting Eradication before Containment, which is exactly the kind of mix-up this distractor represents.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 3, the total time an attacker operates inside an environment before being detected and stopped is called ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 3 introduces dwell time as the real cost of a team that's too slow or too skeptical to confirm a genuine incident — every extra minute of dwell time gives the attacker more time inside the environment.

questions.prompt: Match each component of a real incident response plan, from Lesson 5, to what it actually defines.
right: A legal or contractual deadline, such as GDPR's 72-hour window, triggered by certain types of incidents
The specific threshold and contact for moving a decision to someone with more authority
A defined scale, decided in advance, with concrete criteria for how serious an incident is
Exactly who gets notified, in what order, and within what time window, for each severity level
questions.explain: Severity classification is the predefined scale with concrete per-level criteria; the communication plan is the who/when/order of notification; an escalation path is the specific threshold and contact for moving a decision up the chain; and a breach notification requirement is the external legal deadline, like GDPR's 72 hours, that a plan has to flag — all per Lesson 5's list of core IR plan components.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about incident response playbooks, per Lesson 6.
options: A ransomware playbook calls for isolating affected hosts from the network without powering them off, since powering off can destroy memory-resident evidence
A business email compromise playbook includes notifying finance immediately, since the attacker may have initiated a fraudulent wire transfer by impersonating the compromised employee
A data exfiltration playbook's priority is preserving DLP and proxy logs before they roll off, since legal's notification decision depends on what was actually taken
An insider threat playbook routes straight to technical containment first, the same as an external-attacker playbook, since the technical risk is identical
Any ransom-payment decision should be made unilaterally by whichever technical responder is on call at the time
questions.explain: Lesson 6 is specific about each playbook's priorities: ransomware isolates without powering off, BEC loops in finance over a possible fraudulent wire transfer, and data exfiltration preserves DLP/proxy logs before they age out. Insider threat is the one playbook that requires looping in HR and Legal before any technical action — the opposite of option D — and ransom-payment decisions are explicitly routed through legal, executives, and the insurance carrier, never a unilateral technical call.

questions.prompt: In the RACI model Lesson 7 describes, which statement correctly distinguishes Responsible from Accountable?
options: Responsible is who actually performs the work for a task; Accountable is who owns the decision and answers for the outcome, with exactly one Accountable person per item
Responsible is who owns the decision and answers for the outcome; Accountable is who actually performs the work
Responsible and Accountable both describe people who are only informed after a decision is made, with no input beforehand
Accountable means the same thing as Consulted — both describe someone who gives input before a decision is made
There should be multiple Accountable people per decision, so no single person bears the full outcome
questions.explain: Lesson 7 is precise about this: Responsible is who does the work, Accountable is who owns the decision and answers for the outcome, and there should be exactly one Accountable person per item — collapsing the two, or allowing more than one Accountable person, is exactly the ambiguity RACI exists to remove.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reverses the two roles entirely — it's Accountable, not Responsible, that owns the decision and answers for the outcome, while Responsible is the one doing the hands-on work. Lesson 7's own example shows the technical lead as Responsible for executing isolation while the Incident Commander, not the technical lead, is Accountable for the go-ahead — the exact reversal this distractor represents.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: during a tabletop exercise, a new piece of information the facilitator introduces mid-exercise to evolve the scenario, such as revealing the last backup actually failed eleven days ago, is called an ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 8 defines an inject as exactly this: a new detail the facilitator drops into the scenario as it runs, forcing the team to apply the plan and playbooks to a development nobody had time to prepare for in advance.

questions.prompt: An 'impossible travel' alert is confirmed as a real account takeover. Per Lesson 9, why isn't closing that one alert a complete triage of the incident?
options: Because a real incident is almost never just that one alert — the analyst needs to pull every alert and event tied to the same account into one working set, since the first alert may sit on top of a mailbox rule change, an OAuth grant, or a data download
Because impossible-travel alerts are always false positives and need a second review before being trusted at all
Because the incident can't be confirmed real until the Containment phase has already started
Because triage at incident scale means re-running the same single-alert check a second time on the identical alert
questions.explain: Lesson 9's own example shows exactly this: confirming the impossible-travel alert as real is only the entry point. Pulling every event tied to the same account can turn up a mailbox forwarding rule, an OAuth consent grant, and a file download — a confirmed account takeover with several related events, not a single closed ticket.

questions.prompt: Match each log source from Lesson 10's four-source example to the stage of the attack it revealed.
right: Lateral movement — a remote session opening to a file server
Data staging — a large archive file created in a temp folder
Initial access — a successful sign-in using harvested credentials
The phishing message actually being delivered
questions.explain: In Lesson 10's reconstructed timeline, email security logged the phishing delivery, identity logs showed the initial-access sign-in, endpoint logs on the victim host showed the lateral-movement remote session, and endpoint logs on the file server showed the data-staging archive file — each source holding one piece of a sequence no single system saw in full.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: systematically checking everything else an attacker may have touched — other accounts, other hosts, and whether any data actually left the environment — is called ________, per Lesson 11.
questions.explain: Lesson 11 defines scoping as exactly this systematic check, distinct from just fixing whatever was already found — incomplete scoping is the common failure pattern where a second foothold gets missed and the incident reopens later.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about incident severity classification, per Lesson 12.
options: Severity depends on business impact, data sensitivity, scope/spread, and regulatory implications, not mainly on technical sophistication
Two incidents with nearly identical technical attack chains can land at very different severity levels depending on whose account was compromised and what it could access
A severity level is primarily a filing label and has little real effect on how many people get pulled into the response
Regulatory implications, such as PCI DSS or HIPAA exposure, can turn an otherwise contained technical incident into a critical one
Scope/spread, as a severity factor, is unrelated to the scoping work covered in Lesson 11
questions.explain: Lesson 12 names business impact, data sensitivity, scope/spread, and regulatory implications as the four real drivers of severity — and its own worked example shows the same technical attack chain landing at moderate severity for one account and critical for another, once PCI DSS exposure enters the picture. Severity actively drives resourcing and executive notification, not just a label, and scope/spread is explicitly the direct payoff of Lesson 11's scoping work, not something separate from it.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes short-term containment from long-term containment, per Lesson 13?
options: Short-term containment is a fast, narrow action that stops active damage right now, like isolating a host; long-term containment is a durable response, like rebuilding from a clean image or rotating credentials, that lets the investigation continue safely
Short-term containment rebuilds the affected system from a clean image; long-term containment simply isolates the host from the network
Short-term and long-term containment both refer to the same isolation action, differing only in which team performs them
Long-term containment always happens before short-term containment, since the durable fix has to be ready first
Short-term containment is a formality performed only for compliance audits, with no real effect on an active attacker
Long-term containment means permanently deleting the compromised system without preserving it for forensics
questions.explain: Lesson 13 draws this line clearly: short-term containment is the fast, narrow action — isolate a host, disable an account, block an IP — that stops the bleeding right now. Long-term containment is the slower, durable work that follows: rebuilding from a known-clean image, rotating credentials environment-wide, or standing up a replacement system, all while preserving the original system for forensics.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B swaps the two definitions backwards — rebuilding from a clean image is exactly the long-term containment work Lesson 13 describes, while simple isolation is the short-term action. Treating the fast isolation step as the 'long-term' fix is precisely the mistake the lesson warns against: an isolated host that never gets the long-term rebuild becomes a permanent, forgotten blind spot.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the factors that go into a real isolation decision on a critical system, per Lesson 14.
options: Confidence in how active and spreading the compromise actually is should weigh into the decision
Reversibility — how easily the decision could be undone if it turns out wrong — is a real factor
A compensating control, like blocking one port or disabling one account, can sometimes reduce risk without the full cost of isolating the whole system
Because isolation is a purely technical action, the SOC analyst should always make the final call alone, regardless of the system's business criticality
In genuinely safety- or life-critical environments, patient safety or regulatory duty can outweigh revenue considerations entirely
questions.explain: Lesson 14 lists confidence, spread risk, business impact, reversibility, and the availability of a compensating control as the real factors in an isolation decision, and its hospital-versus-retailer example shows safety outweighing revenue outright in a life-critical setting. The decision explicitly does not rest with the analyst alone on a high-impact system — it routes through a named decision-maker per the IR plan's authorization matrix, which makes option D false.

questions.prompt: Match each containment term from Lesson 15 to what it actually does.
right: The route an attacker keeps open if only one of account or host containment is performed, not both
Disabling a compromised account, forcing a password reset, and revoking active sessions or tokens
Invalidating an already-authenticated session so a stolen token stops working, not just the password
Isolating a compromised machine from the network while leaving it running for investigation
questions.explain: Account containment disables the account and revokes sessions/tokens; host containment isolates the machine; session/token revocation is specifically why a password reset alone isn't enough, since a stolen token can keep working; and the credential-reuse/lateral path is exactly what's left open if only one of the two containment actions is performed, per Lesson 15's phishing-to-cloud-mailbox example.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: documentation of who handled a piece of evidence, when, and how, so its integrity can later be verified by a regulator, court, or insurer, is called ________, per Lesson 16.
questions.explain: Lesson 16 names chain of custody as the documentation that has to accompany a memory dump or disk image — an undocumented gap in that chain can undermine evidence that otherwise would hold up to outside scrutiny.

questions.prompt: Meridian's team runs the commands above to remove the attacker's scheduled task and rogue local account, per Lesson 17. Why would the incident still be unresolved afterward if the team stops there?
options: Because the actual root cause — the unpatched Remote Desktop Gateway that let the attacker in in the first place — is still just as open as it was before, and nothing stops the same or a different attacker from walking back in through it
Because PowerShell's Get- commands never actually confirm whether an item exists before it's removed
Because scheduled tasks and local accounts can only be removed by rebooting the entire domain controller
Because Unregister-ScheduledTask and Remove-LocalUser require the attacker's own credentials to run successfully
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit that eradication is three jobs, not one: removing attacker tooling, closing the vulnerability that let them in, and removing every persistence mechanism. Meridian's root cause was the unpatched Remote Desktop Gateway — cleaning up the scheduled task and rogue account removes what the attacker did after getting in, but leaves the door they walked through exactly as open as before.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for picking and trusting a backup to restore from, per Lesson 18, in the correct order.
items: Determine the earliest confirmed compromise timestamp from the investigation's timeline
Select the most recent backup that predates that timestamp, rather than simply the most recent backup available
Restore that backup to an isolated, non-production environment and run an updated EDR scan against it
Verify the backup's checksums and confirm the backup service account doesn't appear in the incident's compromised credentials
questions.explain: Lesson 18 builds this sequence directly from Meridian's case: the timeline reconstruction work locates the 11:40 PM compromise, which rules out the 1:00 AM Wednesday backup and points to the 1:00 AM Tuesday backup instead; that backup still has to be scanned in isolation before it's trusted, and its checksums and the backup service account's own exposure still have to be checked, since a backup that predates the attack by timestamp but was captured with compromised credentials isn't actually known-good.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four validation checks Lesson 19 describes before a system returns to production.
options: Patch confirmation means verifying the security update is actually installed on the running system, not just scheduled or pushed
The persistence re-check re-runs the same scheduled-task, local-user, and registry checks from Lesson 17, even on hosts already eradicated once
The vulnerability scan should be a general 'looks okay' scan rather than one targeted at the specific CVE that was exploited
A defined monitoring window, like Meridian's 72 hours of elevated monitoring, is one of the four checks
Once eradication is complete, validation is considered optional, since the system has already been confirmed clean
questions.explain: Lesson 19 names patch confirmation, a persistence re-check, a targeted vulnerability scan against the specific exploited CVE, and a defined monitoring window as the four real checks — explicitly not a general scan and explicitly not an optional step, since skipping validation is called out as a common, costly real IR mistake.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: bringing systems back into production in priority-ordered tiers, with monitoring between each group instead of all at once, is called ________ recovery, per Lesson 20.
questions.explain: Lesson 20 names phased recovery as Meridian's approach — Tier 1 domain controllers and infrastructure first, Tier 2 the directly-compromised systems next, Tier 3 end-user workstations last — so that a validation miss on any one system stays contained instead of going live everywhere at once.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 21, which three questions does a real lessons learned meeting have to answer about every phase of the response?
options: What worked? What didn't? What should change?
Who is to blame? What was the financial cost? Who approved the response?
How fast was detection? How fast was containment? How fast was recovery?
What regulations apply? What is the public statement? Who notifies customers?
Was the incident a true positive? Was it a false positive? Was it a benign true positive?
questions.explain: Lesson 21 states the agenda plainly: a lessons learned meeting asks what worked, what didn't, and what should change, about every phase of the response — and every answer to the third question becomes a candidate action item for the after-action report.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C lists MTTD/MTTR-style timing questions, which are real metrics covered later in Lesson 24, but they are not the three questions the lessons learned meeting itself is built to answer. Confusing a speed metric with the meeting's actual what-worked/what-didn't/what-should-change agenda misses the specific purpose Lesson 21 describes.

questions.prompt: Match each section of a real after-action report, per Lesson 22, to what it actually documents.
right: A follow-up fix with a named owner and a specific, checkable deadline
What was actually affected — systems, data, downtime, cost, and reporting obligations
A chronological record from first indicator through recovery completion, in a consistently stated timezone
The actual underlying cause, such as a phished credential or unpatched vulnerability, not just the symptom that triggered the alert
questions.explain: Lesson 22 lays out a real AAR's sections: the incident timeline is the chronological record, root cause is the underlying reason distinct from the triggering symptom, impact is what was actually affected, and action items are the specific, owned, dated fixes — the part the lesson calls out as the one that actually changes anything.

questions.code:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\AppData\\", "\\Temp\\", "\\Users\\Public\\")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine
questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the query above from Lesson 23, the KQL operator ________ is what matches ProcessCommandLine against several suspicious folder paths at once, narrowing a noisy schtasks.exe query into a precise one.
questions.explain: Lesson 23 identifies has_any as the specific operator that narrows the query: the first-pass schtasks.exe query was too broad because legitimate software creates scheduled tasks constantly, and has_any is what restricts it to tasks pointing at AppData, Temp, or Users\Public — the detail that turned the AAR's root cause into a precise, low-noise analytics rule.

questions.prompt: Across three similar business email compromise incidents, MTTR drops from 4 hours 10 minutes, to 2 hours 5 minutes, to 1 hour 50 minutes. Per Lesson 24, why does this trend matter more than any single incident's MTTR number?
options: Because a single incident's MTTR tells you almost nothing on its own — a falling trend across similar incidents is real evidence that the lessons learned meeting, the AAR's action items, and new detections actually, measurably changed how fast the team responds
Because MTTR is only meaningful when it is calculated once per quarter, not tracked per incident
Because a single incident's MTTR is always inflated by the lessons learned meeting that follows it
Because MTTD and MTTR are supposed to stay exactly the same across every incident, so any change signals a measurement error
questions.explain: Lesson 24 walks through exactly this three-incident trend and makes the point directly: a falling MTTR trend, not a single number, is the real evidence that Post-Incident Activity's fixes — the access change, the playbook update, the new Sentinel rule — weren't just paperwork.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 25, which of the following is actually a usable, testable threat hunting hypothesis?
options: An attacker may be using rundll32.exe to load and execute a malicious DLL from a user's Downloads or Temp folder instead of its normal System32 path
Something bad might be happening somewhere on the network
The SOC should look at more logs this week to see what turns up
An attacker is probably doing something suspicious, but it's hard to say exactly what
questions.explain: Lesson 25 draws the line precisely: a usable hypothesis has to be specific and testable, naming a specific binary, behavior, and reason an attacker would use it — exactly what the rundll32.exe/LOLBin hypothesis does. 'Something bad might be happening' is a feeling, not a hypothesis, because there's no query that could prove or disprove it.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the threat hunting loop, per Lesson 26.
options: The loop runs in four stages: form a hypothesis, gather data, analyze, document findings — then refine and repeat
A hunt that comes back with no matching activity found is a wasted, failed hunt
A documented negative finding is still genuinely useful, since it confirms a specific technique isn't present in the environment as of that check
After a hunt, whether it found something or not, the team goes back to stage one with a sharper or new hypothesis
Once a hunt is run one time, the loop is considered finished and doesn't need to be repeated
questions.explain: Lesson 26 names the four stages and is explicit that a clean result is not a failed hunt — it's a documented negative finding that's genuinely useful. The loop's fourth stage, refine and repeat, is exactly why hunting is described as an ongoing practice rather than a task that's ever finished, which rules out both B and D.

questions.prompt: A team's MITRE ATT&CK coverage heat map, per Lesson 27, shows Persistence techniques well hunted but Credential Access techniques completely unshaded. What should the team actually do with that gap?
options: Treat the unshaded Credential Access techniques as a source of the next hypothesis to form and run through the hunting loop, since a coverage gap is itself the next hunt
Ignore Credential Access entirely, since a well-covered Persistence tactic means the environment is already adequately protected
Wait for an actual incident involving Credential Access before hunting for it
Mark the heat map complete, since only Persistence techniques need active hunting coverage
questions.explain: Lesson 27 is direct about this: a coverage gap on the heat map isn't just a record-keeping detail, it's the next hunt — an unshaded Credential Access cell becomes exactly the kind of specific, testable hypothesis the team should form and run next, rather than something to wait on or ignore.

questions.prompt: In the capstone case, Sentinel's impossible-travel rule fires on tmarsh@alderbrookwealth.com at 2:47 PM. Per Lesson 29, what would the SOC have missed if the analyst had disabled Teresa Marsh's account immediately without ever opening the investigation graph?
options: The second compromised asset, WKSTN-FIN-14, where a Defender for Endpoint alert showed a PowerShell process spawned from Outlook downloading a remote-access tool — an active foothold that the sign-in alert alone never named
Nothing — the sign-in alert alone already fully scoped the incident, since Entra ID sign-ins and Defender for Endpoint alerts always correlate automatically
The fact that Teresa Marsh was not actually a real employee of Alderbrook Wealth Partners
The specific KQL query used to build the original impossible-travel analytics rule
questions.explain: Lesson 29 shows the investigation graph linking the Account entity to a Host entity, WKSTN-FIN-14, through a Defender for Endpoint alert raised nine minutes after the foreign sign-in. The original analytics rule only fired on sign-in geography; without opening the graph to scope the incident, the team would disable one account and miss the active foothold still running on that laptop.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about how the capstone's Lesson 30 handled WKSTN-FIN-14 and its after-action report.
options: WKSTN-FIN-14 was restored from a verified-clean backup rather than cleaned live, because SYSTEM-level persistence meant the attacker may have planted something the triage capture didn't catch
The after-action report's follow-up items included enforcing number-matching MFA tenant-wide, because simple approve/deny MFA is what let the push-fatigue sign-in through
Validation before returning the device to production included re-running the same forensic query tenant-wide to confirm the malicious scheduled task's name and tool hash didn't exist anywhere else
Teresa's account was re-enabled immediately after the host was rebuilt, with no password reset needed since the account itself was never actually compromised
The after-action report's follow-up items included enabling Sysmon/Event 4698 auditing, because scheduled-task creation wasn't being logged for alerting
questions.explain: Lesson 30 restores the host from backup specifically because SYSTEM-level persistence could mean something else was planted; validates by re-running the forensic query tenant-wide; and the AAR's follow-ups include number-matching MFA and Sysmon/4698 auditing. Teresa's account was re-enabled only after a forced password reset and MFA re-registration — her account absolutely was compromised, since the attacker used her approved MFA push to get in — which makes option D false.

questions.prompt: Put these events from the capstone case, across Lessons 29 through 31, in the order they actually happened.
items: The impossible-travel analytics rule fires on Teresa Marsh's account at 2:47 PM
Triage confirms a real incident after checking for a VPN exit node, Teresa's travel history, and the approved MFA push
The investigation graph reveals a second compromised asset, WKSTN-FIN-14
Live response captures volatile evidence before the host is isolated and Teresa's account is disabled
A hypothesis-driven hunt for inbox-forwarding rules finds a second compromised account belonging to Daniel Oyelaran
questions.explain: Lesson 29 opens with the 2:47 PM rule firing, then triage confirms it's real, then the investigation graph surfaces WKSTN-FIN-14 as a second asset, then evidence capture happens before isolation and disabling the account. Only after that incident is closed out does Lesson 31's hypothesis-driven hunt, built from the same credential-theft wave, find Daniel Oyelaran's independently compromised account — the sequence the capstone runs end to end.
